get.description: Returns 200 while the HTTP runtime is accepting requests. Requires no authentication and checks no dependency — a failure here means the process should be restarted.

Reports whether critical dependencies are reachable. `200` when every check passes,
`503` when any is down — so a load balancer can drain this instance without restarting it.

Checks that MongoDB answers, and that every index the schemas declare actually exists.

The index check is not decoration. `autoIndex` is off by design, so a database that has
never had `indexes:sync` run against it connects, answers every query, and serves traffic
with several unique constraints simply absent - and those constraints are the entire
enforcement behind "one account per email" and "one order per idempotency key". An
instance in that state must refuse traffic rather than accept it and violate them.

Every address saved by the signed-in customer, **default first**, then oldest first, with
the id as a final tie-break. That order is total, so the list is stable between requests.

A customer who has never saved one gets an empty array, not a `404`.

Not paginated: the book is capped at **10 addresses**, so a
page cursor would describe a boundary that cannot be crossed.

At most one entry has `isDefault: true`. Zero is also valid — a customer who deleted their
last address has no default until they save another.

403.description: FORBIDDEN — an address book belongs to a CUSTOMER account.

post.description:
Adds one address to the book and returns it, including the `id` you will send to
`POST /orders`.

### The default

- The **first** address you save becomes the default automatically — a customer with
  addresses and no default has nothing for a checkout screen to pre-select.
- A later address does **not** disturb the existing default unless you send
  `isDefault: true`, which unsets the current one in the same atomic write.

When you send `isDefault: true` the response tells you the whole story: this address is
now the default, so every other one is not. No refetch is needed.

### Limits

At most **10** saved addresses. The 11th
returns `422 ADDRESS_LIMIT_REACHED` — delete one first.

The address is stored exactly as typed. Nothing here verifies that the street exists or
that a courier can reach it: no geocoder and no address-verification vendor is integrated,
and pretending otherwise would be claiming something the server cannot know.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — a field is missing, too long, or the phone is not an Egyptian mobile number. UNKNOWN_FIELD — the body carried a field this endpoint does not accept, such as `userId` or `id`.

403.description: FORBIDDEN — addresses belong to CUSTOMER accounts. ACCOUNT_DISABLED.

422.description: ADDRESS_LIMIT_REACHED — the address book is full.

get.description:
One saved address, by id.

An address belonging to another customer returns **404**, exactly as an id that does not
exist anywhere does. The two are indistinguishable on purpose: a `403` would confirm that
the id is real and turn this endpoint into an oracle for somebody else’s address book.

A malformed id is a `400` instead, which discloses nothing — it depends only on the
characters you sent.

parameters.name: addressId
parameters.description: 24-character hex id of one of YOUR saved addresses.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — `addressId` is not a 24-character hex string.

404.description: ADDRESS_NOT_FOUND — no such address, or it is not yours. The same answer for both.

patch.description:
A partial update: send only the fields you are changing. An omitted field is left exactly
as it was. Send `postalCode: null` to clear it.

### This cannot change a past order

An order stores its own **immutable copy** of the address it was placed against. Editing
the saved address here changes where your NEXT order goes and nothing about where an
earlier one went — an invoice must still say what it said on the day.

### `isDefault` is not accepted here

Sending it returns `400 UNKNOWN_FIELD`. Making an address default is a write against every
OTHER address, not against this one, so it has its own endpoint that performs it in a
single atomic update: `POST /users/me/addresses/{addressId}/default`.

parameters.name: addressId
parameters.description: 24-character hex id of one of YOUR saved addresses.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — a supplied field is invalid, or `addressId` is malformed. UNKNOWN_FIELD — the body carried `isDefault`, `userId` or another field this endpoint does not accept.

404.description: ADDRESS_NOT_FOUND — no such address, or it is not yours.

delete.description:
Removes the address from the book. It affects **future use only**.

### What deleting does NOT do

It does not delete, alter or hide any order. It does not touch an order’s address
snapshot, its items, its totals, its inventory movements or its shipment record. Every
past order remains fully renderable, because none of them reads this document.

For the same reason there is no "this address is used by an order" refusal: nothing
depends on it, so blocking the delete would protect nothing.

### If you delete the default

A replacement is promoted **deterministically** — the oldest surviving address, with the
id as a tie-break — so the outcome is a documented rule rather than an accident of
storage order. Delete your last address and you simply have no default.

Returns the **whole remaining book**, because the default may have moved to an address you
did not name. Replace your local list with it.

Not idempotent: deleting the same id twice returns `404` the second time, which is the same
answer somebody else’s id would get.

parameters.name: addressId
parameters.description: 24-character hex id of one of YOUR saved addresses.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — `addressId` is not a 24-character hex string.

404.description: ADDRESS_NOT_FOUND — no such address, or it is not yours.

post.description:
Sets this address as the default and, **in the same atomic update**, unsets whichever
address currently holds it. There is no window in which two are default and none in which
zero are: the whole array is rewritten once, and MongoDB applies that rewrite atomically.
Concurrent requests naming different addresses therefore leave exactly one default —
whichever landed last — never two.

Repeating it on the address that is already default is a no-op and still returns `200`.

Returns the **whole book**, because this operation changes addresses you did not name.
Replace your local list with it rather than merging.

The default is a pre-selection for a checkout screen. It is never applied automatically:
`POST /orders` always names the address it is shipping to.

parameters.name: addressId
parameters.description: 24-character hex id of one of YOUR saved addresses.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — `addressId` is not a 24-character hex string.

404.description: ADDRESS_NOT_FOUND — no such address, or it is not yours.

post.summary: Make one of my addresses the default

patch.description:
Partial update of the signed-in customer. Returns the whole profile as it now stands.

**Omitting a key leaves that field unchanged.** For `phone`, `null` is a different
instruction from omission: it removes the number.

`email`, `role` and verification state are **not** editable here. Sending any of them
returns `400 UNKNOWN_FIELD` — changing a login identifier requires proving the new
address, and role is server-owned.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR, or UNKNOWN_FIELD for a field that is not editable.

403.description: FORBIDDEN — a profile belongs to a CUSTOMER account.

404.description: RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND — the account was deleted while the token was still valid.

post.description:
Creates a `CUSTOMER` account and issues an email-verification challenge.

**No session is returned.** The account must be verified before it can sign in, so the
client should show a "check your email" state rather than navigating to a guarded route.

The `role` field does not exist on this DTO. Sending one returns `400 UNKNOWN_FIELD`.

Rate limited to 3 requests per hour per IP.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR (including password policy) or UNKNOWN_FIELD.

409.description: DUPLICATE_EMAIL

post.description:
Returns an access/refresh token pair and the canonical user object.

**An unknown email and a wrong password are indistinguishable** — same status, same code,
same message, and the same wall-clock time. Do not build UI that tries to tell them apart.

`EMAIL_NOT_VERIFIED` and `ACCOUNT_DISABLED` are reachable only AFTER a correct password,
so they are safe to surface: they inform the account holder without informing an enumerator.

Rate limited to 5 attempts per 15 minutes, per IP **and** email.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR

post.description:
Exchanges a refresh token for a NEW access/refresh pair. The presented refresh token is
invalidated by this call — refresh tokens are strictly single-use.

**Client contract.** Store the new `refreshToken` before retrying the original request. If
two requests refresh concurrently, one wins and the other receives
`REFRESH_TOKEN_INVALID`; serialise refreshes behind a single in-flight future.

**`REFRESH_TOKEN_REUSED` is terminal.** Presenting an already-rotated token is treated as
theft: the entire rotation chain is revoked. Clear stored tokens and send the user to sign
in — do not retry.

Public because the access token is, by definition, already expired when this is called.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR

post.description:
Revokes the presented refresh token. **Idempotent**: an unknown or already-revoked token
still returns 200, because the caller’s intent — "this session must not work" — is
already satisfied.

Public, and takes the refresh token in the body, so a client holding an expired access
token can still sign out cleanly. The access token itself is not revocable; it expires on
its own within 15 minutes.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR

post.description: Revokes every live refresh token for the authenticated user, on every device. Outstanding access tokens remain valid for at most their 15-minute lifetime.

get.description:
Returns the canonical user object — the same shape embedded in the login response.

Never returns `passwordHash`, `tokenVersion` or any verification state beyond the
`emailVerified` boolean: those fields do not exist on this DTO.

post.description: Consumes the single-use token from the verification email. Expired and unknown tokens are reported identically. Delivery of that email arrives with the notifications module.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — token invalid or expired.

post.description:
**Always returns 200**, whether or not the address exists or is already verified.
Anything else would make this a password-free account-existence oracle.

Issuing a new challenge invalidates the previous one.

Rate limited to 3 requests per hour, per IP **and** email.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR

post.description:
**Always returns 200**, with the same body, whether or not the address has an account.
Anything else would make this a password-free account-existence oracle — an attacker with
a list of addresses would learn which ones are registered here.

The token is 32 random bytes, stored only as a SHA-256 digest, single-use, and valid for
one hour. Requesting again invalidates the previous link.

Rate limited to 3 requests per hour, per IP **and** email — the same limit as registration,
because this endpoint also causes an email to be sent to an address the caller names.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR

post.description:
Consumes the single-use token and sets the new password. Unknown, expired and
already-used tokens are reported identically.

On success this **signs the account out everywhere**: `tokenVersion` is incremented,
which invalidates every outstanding access token, and every refresh token is revoked.
Both happen in one transaction with the credential change — a reset that left an
attacker's session alive would not have reset anything.

The new password must satisfy the full server-side policy, including not containing the
account's own email address.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — token invalid or expired, or the password is refused.

get.description:
The main discovery endpoint. Returns a page of products, the TRUE total match count and
server-computed facets — all in one round trip.

**Filters combine with AND.** `brand` is repeatable and ORs within itself; `spec` is
repeatable and ANDs across keys while ORing within one key.

**`category` matches the whole subtree**, so a parent category includes every descendant
category's products. An unknown category slug returns 404; an unknown brand slug simply
narrows the result set to nothing.

**Facet counts reflect the filters currently applied**, because they are computed over the
filtered set. `facets.priceRange` is the range across all matches, not the current page.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based page number.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Items per page, 1–100.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Free-text search across name, SKU, brand and descriptions. SKU is weighted almost as highly as the name, so an exact part number matches first. Absent or empty = browse mode.

parameters.name: category
parameters.description: Category slug. Matches the ENTIRE SUBTREE, so a parent category includes every descendant category’s products.

parameters.name: brand
parameters.description: Brand slug. Repeatable: `?brand=espressif&brand=arduino` is an OR within brands.

parameters.name: minPrice
parameters.description: Minimum price in integer minor units (piastres), applied to the EFFECTIVE price (salePrice ?? basePrice) — the same value checkout charges.

parameters.name: maxPrice
parameters.description: Maximum effective price in integer minor units (piastres).

parameters.name: inStock
parameters.description: When true, returns only products with stock on hand.

parameters.name: featured
parameters.description: When true, returns only featured products. Useful for a home-screen rail.

parameters.name: spec
parameters.description: Spec facet filter as `key:value`. Repeatable. AND across different keys, OR within one key: `?spec=operating-voltage:3.3&spec=connectivity:Wi-Fi` means voltage 3.3 AND Wi-Fi.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Sort order. Defaults to `relevance` when `q` is present and `newest` otherwise. Requesting `relevance` without `q` falls back to `newest` rather than erroring. Any other value returns 400 UNSUPPORTED_SORT.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR, UNKNOWN_FIELD or UNSUPPORTED_SORT.

404.description: CATEGORY_NOT_FOUND — unknown `category` slug.

get.description: Up to 8 lightweight results for a search-as-you-type box. Anchored PREFIX match on product name and SKU — makers search by part number, so SKU is matched first-class.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Prefix to match against product name and SKU.

get.description:
Full detail by public slug, including every image and every spec. Inactive and
soft-deleted products return 404 — identical to a slug that never existed, so an id can
never become an existence oracle.

**A slug that has been renamed answers `301` with a `Location` header** pointing at the
current one (CATALOG-MODEL.md §2 rule 4, ADR-CATALOG-005). The redirect is a FALLBACK:
a live slug is resolved first and never consults the redirect table, so a slug that has
been re-used by a different product resolves to that product rather than to wherever the
previous holder went.

Legacy wrote these redirect rows on every rename and **nothing ever read one**, so every
rename produced a permanent 404 with a database row recording exactly where the page had
gone. That is defect K4, and this lookup is the half that was missing.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Lowercase kebab-case public identifier.

301.description: The slug was renamed. `Location` carries the current URL; the body repeats the target slug so a client that does not follow redirects can still act on it.

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND

get.description: Up to 8 products in the same category, excluding this one, ordered by sales.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Lowercase kebab-case public identifier.

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND

get.description: Flat list of every visible category, ordered by depth then sort order. Each row carries `parentId` and `depth`, so a client can assemble the tree itself if it prefers.
The nested navigation tree, roots first. Assembled in memory from a single read and cached for 15 minutes. Maximum depth is 3.
Detail plus the ancestor trail, root first. To list this category’s products — including every descendant category’s — call `GET /products?category={slug}`.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Lowercase kebab-case public identifier.

404.description: CATEGORY_NOT_FOUND

get.description: Flat alphabetical list. Brands are a filter dimension, not a required taxonomy — most products have none, so never require one in the UI.
To list this brand’s products, call `GET /products?brand={slug}`.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Lowercase kebab-case public identifier.

404.description: BRAND_NOT_FOUND

get.description:
Answers whether a slug is available for a product, category or brand, and offers the
next free alternative when it is not — `esp32-devkit-2`, per CATALOG-MODEL.md §2.

Pass `excludeId` when EDITING an existing entity, or it will report its own slug as
taken and every save of an unchanged product will be refused.

**This endpoint fails closed.** The admin route it replaces answered "available" on
every failure path — a database error, a missing service, any exception — so a check
that could not reach the database told the operator their slug was free. The form is
built to trust this answer, which makes a wrong "available" worse than no check at all.
A failure here is a 5xx.

A soft-deleted entity still holds its slug. Reusing it would silently repoint every
existing link to a different product.

parameters.name: slug
parameters.description: Lowercase alphanumerics separated by single hyphens, no leading or trailing hyphen.

parameters.name: excludeId
parameters.description: The entity being EDITED. Without it, saving an unchanged product reports its own slug as taken and the save is refused.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — a malformed slug or an unknown `type`. UNKNOWN_FIELD — an undocumented query parameter.

get.description:
Every product including **drafts** — `isActive: false` rows a customer cannot see. Soft-
deleted products are EXCLUDED unless `?state=deleted` asks for them: a recoverable
deletion has to be findable, but mixing deleted rows into the working list is how
somebody edits a product no customer can reach and does not notice for a week.

`?q=` matches SKU, slug and English name anywhere in the value — an operator typing
"esp32" expects "ESP32-WROOM-32", which a tokenised text index would not return. The
term is escaped before it reaches the database.

`?lowStock=true` lists products at or below their own threshold, which is a per-product
number and not one global constant.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based page number.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Items per page, 1–100.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Matches SKU, slug and English name, case-insensitively. ESCAPED before it reaches the database — no character in it can mean anything to a query expression.

parameters.name: categoryId
parameters.description: Exact category, not the subtree.

parameters.name: lowStock
parameters.description: Only products at or below their low-stock threshold.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR / UNKNOWN_FIELD.

get.summary: The catalogue, as an operator sees it

post.description:
**Created UNPUBLISHED by default.** `isActive` defaults to `false` here, against the
schema default of `true`, because a product created through this endpoint has no images
and no stock yet — publishing it at the instant it is named puts a bare row in a
customer’s search results. Publish is a separate, separately audited action.

**`stock` is not accepted, and sending it is a 400.** InventoryModule is the sole writer
of stock (CATALOG-MODEL.md §4) because every movement must produce a ledger event. A
generic product write that could set `stock.onHand` is legacy defect M7 exactly. New
products start at zero and receive stock through an inventory adjustment, which ledgers it.

Also rejected, each for its own reason: `effectivePrice` (maintained — `salePrice ??
basePrice`; a caller that could set it independently could make the sortable price
disagree with the charged one), `rating` and `salesCount` (owned by other modules), and
`images` (attaching an asset is reference-counted and has its own endpoint — a descriptor
accepted here would point a product at an asset nothing had retained, which is exactly
the state that lets a live image be deleted).

The category and brand SNAPSHOTS are built server-side from the referenced documents.
They are not accepted from the caller: a snapshot a client could write is one that can
disagree with its source.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — a malformed field, or `salePrice` at or above `basePrice`. UNKNOWN_FIELD — a field this endpoint does not accept, including `stock`.

404.description: CATEGORY_NOT_FOUND / BRAND_NOT_FOUND — including a soft-deleted one.

409.description: DUPLICATE_SKU or DUPLICATE_SLUG. `details[0].field` names which, so the form marks the right box. A soft-deleted product still holds both.

get.description:
The editor’s view: both language fields unresolved, `costPrice` present, `deletedAt`
present. This is `ProductAdminDto` in CATALOG-MODEL.md §5 — a SEPARATE type from the
public one, which is what guarantees a margin can never reach a customer. No runtime
field-stripping is involved, so there is no option anyone can get wrong.

A soft-deleted product resolves normally here. It must: the restore action is reached
from its own page.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — `id` is not a 24-character hex id.

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND.

patch.description:
A PARTIAL update. An absent key means "leave it"; an explicit `null`, where the field is
nullable, means "clear it" — which is how a sale is ended (`salePrice: null`) and how a
brand is removed.

**`sku` is not accepted.** CATALOG-MODEL.md §2 makes it immutable after creation: it is
the warehouse identifier, printed on labels and quoted in supplier correspondence, and a
system that lets it change is one where two people are holding different names for one
part.

**`isActive` is not accepted either.** Publishing has its own endpoints because it has
its own audit codes — a visibility flip buried inside a general edit would be recorded as
`PRODUCT_UPDATED`, and "when did this go live" would stop being answerable from the
action index.

**Renaming the slug writes a redirect.** The old slug is recorded in `slugRedirects` and
`GET /products/{oldSlug}` answers `301` thereafter (§2 rules 3–5). Chains are collapsed
at write time: rename A→B then B→C and A points straight at C, so resolution is always
one hop with no cycle to guard.

`salePrice` is validated against the RESULTING pair, not against what was sent — lowering
`basePrice` below an untouched `salePrice` is refused, because both fields are
individually valid and the product would end up "on sale" above list.

Editing a soft-deleted product is refused with `409 PRODUCT_DELETED`: restore it first.
An edit nobody can see is the same problem as the deleted rows the listing keeps out of
its default view.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — a malformed field, or a resulting `salePrice` at or above `basePrice`. UNKNOWN_FIELD — `sku`, `isActive`, `stock`, `images` or any other field this endpoint does not accept.

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND / CATEGORY_NOT_FOUND / BRAND_NOT_FOUND.

409.description: DUPLICATE_SLUG — another entity holds it. PRODUCT_DELETED — restore it first.

delete.description:
Sets `deletedAt` **and** `isActive: false`, per CATALOG-MODEL.md §9. Both, because they
answer different questions and a restore has to tell them apart: after this, "was it
published" is unambiguously no, so bringing it back in front of customers becomes a
separate, separately audited decision rather than something a restore does silently.

The deletion is SOFT and the reasons are §9’s: analytics, reviews and reporting still
resolve the product id; SKUs and slugs must not become silently reusable, because reusing
one repoints every existing link at a different product; and an accidental deletion is
recoverable.

The product keeps its slug, and its `slugRedirects` rows are KEPT. Dropping them would
make a restore silently lose every old URL that worked the day before.

Deleting an already-deleted product is `409`, not `200`. A caller that receives success
twice cannot tell whether it deleted once or twice, and the second answer would carry a
`deletedAt` belonging to somebody else’s action.

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND.

409.description: PRODUCT_DELETED — already deleted.

post.description:
Sets `isActive: true` and audits it as `PRODUCT_PUBLISHED`.

Its own endpoint rather than a field, because AUDIT-MODEL.md §3 audits publication state
separately from an ordinary edit. That is what makes "when did this go live, and who put
it there" one indexed query rather than a scan of every product update ever made.

Idempotent, and SILENT when it is a no-op: publishing an already-published product
succeeds and writes no audit row, because a row recording that nothing changed is noise
in a log kept for two years.

A soft-deleted product is refused — restore is the operation that means "put this back",
and it is audited as one.

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND.

409.description: PRODUCT_DELETED — restore it first.

post.description:
Sets `isActive: false` and audits it as `PRODUCT_UNPUBLISHED`. The product keeps its
slug, its SKU and its stock; it simply stops being publicly readable, along with its
images and specs — CATALOG-MODEL.md §9, "child resources inherit the parent’s
visibility", which is legacy defect Z6 where seven child tables leaked unreleased
products.

This is NOT deletion, and the difference matters to an operator: an unpublished product
is still in the working list, still editable, and still counted. A deleted one is not.

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND.

409.description: PRODUCT_DELETED.

post.description:
Clears `deletedAt`. The product comes back as a **draft** — `isActive` stays false.

Restoring does not republish, and that is deliberate. Putting a product back in front of
customers is a publication decision that AUDIT-MODEL.md §3 audits separately; a restore
that also republished would record "restored" while doing the thing the
`PRODUCT_PUBLISHED` index exists to be the record of. It also means the operator gets to
look at the product before customers do, which is usually why it was deleted.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — the product is not deleted, so there is nothing to restore.

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND.

post.description:
Takes a `publicId` from `POST /admin/media` and, at most, an `alt`. **Every other field
comes from the ledger** — width, height, format, bytes and version. MEDIA-MODEL.md §4:
the browser is never the authority for media metadata. A client that could send
dimensions could make a product page reserve the wrong space; one that could send a
version could point the delivery URL at a generation the CDN has replaced.

**This is what makes the image undeletable while it is in use.** The attach increments the
asset’s reference count, and `DELETE /admin/media` refuses any asset whose count is above
zero. Before this endpoint existed nothing had ever called `retain()`, so every count in
the system sat at zero — harmless while no product had an image, and a live defect the
moment one did.

The first image on a product becomes its primary automatically: §8 requires exactly one
when the array is non-empty, and leaving the first upload non-primary would render a
placeholder on every grid until somebody noticed a radio button.

Attaching the same asset twice is a `409`, not a no-op. A silent second attach would
either double-count the reference — leaving the asset undeletable forever — or skip the
retain and leave the count one short, making it deletable while a live page shows it.
Both are silent; this is not.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR / UNKNOWN_FIELD.

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND. MEDIA_ASSET_NOT_FOUND — the id is not in the ledger.

409.description: PRODUCT_IMAGE_LIMIT — eight already. PRODUCT_IMAGE_ALREADY_ATTACHED. PRODUCT_DELETED — restore it first.

post.summary: Attach an uploaded image to a product

delete.description:
Releases the reference and removes the descriptor. **It never destroys the asset.** One
that falls to zero references is a CANDIDATE for cleanup, reported by
`GET /admin/media/reconciliation` — MEDIA-MODEL.md §9 is explicit that reconciliation
reports rather than deletes, because an automated deleter that misreads state destroys
production assets irreversibly. The same asset may also still be attached elsewhere.

If the image removed was the primary, the first remaining one becomes primary. Leaving a
product with images and no primary renders a placeholder on every grid — K10’s symptom,
reached by a different route.

`publicId` is a query parameter rather than a path segment because it contains slashes:
a path segment would have to be double-encoded by every caller, and a caller that forgot
would silently address a different route.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR.

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND. PRODUCT_IMAGE_NOT_FOUND — not on this product.

409.description: PRODUCT_DELETED.

delete.summary: Remove an image from a product

put.description:
Two legacy defects disappear together here, and both were "the array was written in
pieces":

- **K9** — reordering was an N+1 update loop, one statement per image, so an interrupted
  reorder left an order that was neither the old one nor the new.
- **K10** — "make this the primary" was two statements, unset then set, so an interruption
  between them left a product with NO primary image and every grid rendering a placeholder.

The whole array is written in a single `$set`. CATALOG-MODEL.md §8 asks for exactly this.

The request must name exactly the images the product already has. That restriction is what
makes this operation incapable of changing a reference count — attach and detach are the
only two endpoints that touch the ledger, so there is one place to be right about it
rather than three.

POSITION is the order. `sortOrder` is assigned from the index rather than accepted, because
two entries a client numbered identically would produce an order the database resolves
arbitrarily.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — the list does not match the product’s images, repeats one, or names more than one primary.

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND. PRODUCT_IMAGE_NOT_FOUND.

409.description: PRODUCT_DELETED.

put.summary: Reorder, re-caption and choose the primary — in one atomic write

delete.description:
CATALOG-MODEL.md §9: "Hard delete exists only as a `SUPER_ADMIN` operation for a product
**never referenced by any order**, and it destroys the associated Cloudinary assets."
Every clause of that sentence is a separate guard.

**SUPER_ADMIN only** — an ADMIN gets 403 here and 200 on the soft delete beside it.

**Never ordered.** Orders embed product snapshots, so the commercial record survives
regardless — but every line keeps `productId` for traceability and reorder, and destroying
the document turns that into a dangling id that analytics and the reorder button both
follow to nothing. A referenced product is refused with a count, and soft delete is the
answer for it. That is what soft delete is for.

**The images are destroyed — except the ones another product is showing.** Each is
released; only those that fall to zero references are destroyed in the store. Legacy
destroyed the object regardless of who else pointed at it, and the surviving product
rendered a broken image with no indication of why (W4). The response names both lists.

The product’s `slugRedirects` rows are removed here and ONLY here: a soft delete keeps
them because the product is coming back, and this is the one operation after which the
destination genuinely no longer exists.

403.description: FORBIDDEN — SUPER_ADMIN only. An ADMIN may soft-delete and nothing more.

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND.

409.description: PRODUCT_HAS_ORDERS — `details` names how many. Use the soft delete.

get.description:
Flat rather than nested, because this is the editor’s list: each row carries its own
`parentId`, `path` and `depth`, so a console can assemble whatever shape it wants without
a second request. The nested version customers see is `GET /categories/tree`.

Inactive categories are always included — an operator has to be able to find the one they
hid. Soft-deleted ones need `?includeDeleted=true`.

parameters.name: includeDeleted
parameters.description: Include soft-deleted rows. Excluded by default: a recoverable deletion has to be findable, but the working list is what an operator is editing.

post.description:
`path` and `depth` are computed from `parentId` and are NOT accepted. `path` is the
materialised ancestor chain that makes "every product in this subtree" one indexed match
(ADR-CATALOG-004); a caller-supplied one is a chain that can disagree with `parentId`,
and every subtree query would then be answering from the disagreement.

The depth limit is `3` — MONGODB-DESIGN.md §5. CATALOG-MODEL.md §6 phrases the same limit
as "max 3 levels"; the two reconcile because §6’s own table records the live tree at
**depth** 2, so "levels" there is loose phrasing for the depth §5 names. The reading is
recorded rather than assumed.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — a malformed field, or a parent that would exceed the depth limit.

404.description: CATEGORY_NOT_FOUND — the parent, including a soft-deleted one.

409.description: DUPLICATE_SLUG.

404.description: CATEGORY_NOT_FOUND.

patch.description:
**Three things move when one category does, and this endpoint moves all three.**

1. The category’s own `path` and `depth`, and every descendant’s. `path[]` is materialised
   because MongoDB has no recursive CTE; the price is that a reparent rewrites the subtree
   by hand.
2. Every product’s `category` snapshot — name, slug and the subtree `path`. §6 names the
   mechanism (`updateMany({"category.id": X}, …)`) and calls the staleness window one
   operation on a display label. A rename that skipped this would leave every product card
   showing the old name until something else rewrote it, and nothing else does.
3. The cached category list, which is otherwise fifteen minutes stale.

**Cycle detection is mandatory** (§6). A category cannot become its own parent, and cannot
be moved underneath one of its own subcategories. A cycle makes `path[]` unwritable —
there is no finite ancestor chain — and every tree read afterwards either loops or
silently drops the branch.

The depth limit is checked against the **deepest descendant**, not against this category:
moving a two-level subtree down one level is legal only if the bottom of it still fits.

Renaming the slug writes a `slugRedirects` row, exactly as a product rename does.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — a malformed field, a move that would create a cycle, or one that would push a descendant past the depth limit.

404.description: CATEGORY_NOT_FOUND.

409.description: DUPLICATE_SLUG. CATEGORY_DELETED — restore it first.

delete.description:
Refused with `409 CATEGORY_NOT_EMPTY` while products or live subcategories still point at
it, and the message names both counts so the refusal is a work list rather than a wall.

A cascade was rejected. It would soft-delete a subtree in one click with no way for the
operator to know what went with it — and every product left behind would be filed under a
category that renders nowhere, which is the exact state `POST /admin/catalog/products`
already refuses to create. Allowing it here would make that state reachable by another door.

404.description: CATEGORY_NOT_FOUND.

409.description: CATEGORY_NOT_EMPTY — products or subcategories still belong to it. CATEGORY_DELETED — already deleted.

parameters.description: Include soft-deleted rows. Excluded by default: a recoverable deletion has to be findable, but the working list is what an operator is editing.

404.description: BRAND_NOT_FOUND.

Unlike a category, this is NOT refused when products reference the brand — and the
asymmetry is the design, not an oversight. `product.brand` is nullable: 53 of 85 live
products have no brand and every listing already renders without one, so a product whose
brand goes away lands in a state the whole system handles.

Their `brand` snapshot is therefore CLEARED. Leaving it would put a filter in the brand
facet that returns products whose brand page 404s. How many products were un-branded is
recorded in the audit metadata, because it is the consequence the operator did not
explicitly ask for.

409.description: BRAND_DELETED — already deleted.

post.description:
Accepts `multipart/form-data` with a `file` part and the `entity` / `entityId` fields
naming what the asset is for.

**The server sees every byte** (ADR-MEDIA-001). It is checked against the size limit and
the MIME allow-list, then **sniffed** — a file declaring `image/png` whose contents are
not PNG is refused. It is then decoded, its EXIF orientation baked into the pixels, its
metadata stripped, its long edge capped and its real dimensions read, before anything is
stored. **The client is never the authority for any of it.**

**The response has no `url` and never will.** Build the delivery URL from `publicId` and
`version`; storing a rendered URL turns a CDN change into a data migration.

**The original filename is discarded.** The server generates the identifier.

file.description: JPEG, PNG or WebP, at most 5 MB.

400.description: INVALID_UPLOAD — no file part, an empty file, over the size limit, a MIME type outside the allow-list, contents that contradict the declared type, or an image whose shorter edge is under 200px. `details[0].message` says which. VALIDATION_ERROR — `entity` or `entityId` is malformed.

Permanently removes the asset from the store. **Refused with `409` while anything still
references it** — the reference count is consulted first, and the error names how many
documents would break.

That refusal is the point of the reference ledger. Legacy duplication copied image URLs,
so two products shared one storage object and deleting from either destroyed it for both.

`publicId` is a **query parameter**, not a path segment, because it contains slashes.

parameters.description: The provider-relative identifier, exactly as it was returned by the upload.

Compares the store against the reference ledger in both directions and **reports**.

**Nothing is deleted, by design** (MEDIA-MODEL.md §9.3). An automated deleter that
misreads state destroys assets irreversibly; a report an admin acts on is the right trade
at this scale. Revisit above ~10,000 assets.

parameters.description: Maximum entries per section. A report is read by a person, so it is bounded.

get.description:
Returns the cart, **re-priced and re-checked against live catalogue data on every**
**request**. Stored numbers are never returned.

A customer who has never added anything gets an empty cart, not a 404 — the underlying
document is created lazily on the first add.

Lines whose product went out of stock or was delisted are KEPT and flagged rather than
deleted, so the customer can see why the total changed. They are excluded from
`itemsSubtotal` and set `hasBlockingIssues`.

403.description: FORBIDDEN — carts belong to CUSTOMER accounts.

delete.description: Idempotent, including for a customer who has never had a cart.

post.description:
`quantity` is **additive**: sending 2 for a product already at 3 gives 5. There is never
more than one line per product, under any amount of concurrency.

The result is capped at `min(99, available stock)`. A cap is **not silent** — the response
carries the resulting `quantity` and flags the line `REDUCED_STOCK` when stock was the
binding constraint, so the client can tell the customer.

Returns 200 with the whole cart rather than 201: the resource being returned is the cart,
which already existed or was created implicitly, not a separately addressable line.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR, or UNKNOWN_FIELD if the body carries a price, currency or userId.

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND

409.description: OUT_OF_STOCK — nothing on hand; `details` names the SKU and the available quantity. PRODUCT_UNAVAILABLE — the product is delisted or deleted.

post.summary: Add a product to the cart

patch.description:
`quantity` here is **absolute**, not a delta, and is clamped to available stock.

`0` is rejected by validation: removing a line is `DELETE`, which is idempotent, whereas
a 0 would quietly overload this endpoint with two different meanings.

Returns `404 CART_ITEM_NOT_FOUND` when the product is not already in the cart — use
`POST /cart/items` to add it.

parameters.name: productId
parameters.description: The product id, as returned by the catalogue.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR or UNKNOWN_FIELD

404.description: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND, or CART_ITEM_NOT_FOUND when the product is not in this cart.

409.description: OUT_OF_STOCK or PRODUCT_UNAVAILABLE

delete.description: **Idempotent**: removing a product that is not in the cart still returns 200 with the cart, because the caller’s intent is already satisfied. Returns the whole cart rather than 204 so the client gets the recomputed subtotal without a second round trip.

parameters.name: productId
parameters.description: The product id, as returned by the catalogue.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR

post.description:
Prices a visitor’s browser-held basket and returns it in **the same shape as**
`GET /cart`, so a client renders one component for signed-in and anonymous visitors.

Nothing is stored. No cart document is created, no stock is reserved, and calling it
twice leaves no trace of either call.

### Same resolution as a real cart

Prices, names, images and availability are read from the catalogue on every request, and
quantities are clamped to live stock with the same status ladder — so a basket does not
change shape when its owner signs in.

### Except that no line can be `PRICE_CHANGED`

That status compares the live price against the price the customer was shown when they
added the line, which a stored cart keeps as a snapshot. A browser basket has no such
snapshot, so the comparison genuinely cannot be made and is not faked. Lines are
`OK`, `REDUCED_STOCK`, `OUT_OF_STOCK` or `UNAVAILABLE`.

Duplicate products in `items` are summed, matching what posting the same product twice
to a real cart does. An empty array returns an empty cart rather than an error.

### An id it will not price is an id it says nothing about

A product that is delisted, soft-deleted or simply not real all produce the SAME line: 
`UNAVAILABLE`, an empty `name`, `sku` and `slug`, a zero `unitPrice` and a zero
`availableQuantity`. This endpoint is public, and answering differently for a hidden
product would turn it into a way to enumerate the unpublished catalogue.

A client should therefore treat an `UNAVAILABLE` line with an empty `name` as "this is no
longer for sale" and offer to remove it, rather than showing a blank row. A stored cart
(`GET /cart`) still names such a line, because there the customer added it while it was
real and the cart kept a snapshot.

### Limits

At most 50 distinct products per request, and 120 requests per minute per IP. Both exist because this is an unauthenticated route that reads the catalogue: a basket needs
neither, and a scraper needs both.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR (a malformed id, a quantity out of range, too many lines).

post.description:
Returns the **authoritative** money breakdown for the signed-in customer’s cart, with
per-line status flags. Every figure is recomputed from live catalogue data on this
request; nothing stored is returned, and the client never adds anything up itself.

### What this is NOT

- **Not a reservation.** No stock is held. Another customer may buy the last unit one
  millisecond later.
- **Not a lock, and not a payment authorisation.**
- **Not a promise that `POST /orders` will succeed.** Placement independently revalidates
  everything inside a transaction and may still return `409 OUT_OF_STOCK`.
- **Not persisted.** There is no quote id and nothing to send back. Placement ignores any
  totals a client might have kept.

### Reading the result

- `canPlaceOrder` — whether placement would be accepted right now. Use it for the button.
- `pricing.grandTotal` — the cash amount due on delivery. **Never compute this locally.**
- `pricing.shippingFee` is computed by the server. Pass `addressId` and it is quoted
  against that address governorate — the same calculation `POST /orders` applies, so the
  two agree. Omit it before the customer has chosen an address. `discountTotal` is always
  `0` in this release: no coupon domain exists yet.
- A `PRICE_CHANGED` line is included at the NEW price — compare `unitPrice` with
  `previousUnitPrice` to tell the customer before they commit.

POST rather than GET because the frozen contract shapes this as a body-carrying request.
It has **no side effects** and writes nothing.

The body accepts `addressId` and nothing else. Sending `couponCode` returns
`400 UNKNOWN_FIELD` rather than being silently ignored, so a client is never left believing
it applied a discount that was never validated; a raw `governorate` is refused for a second
reason — the saved address is the authority for it, and accepting free text would let a
client shop for a cheaper delivery fee.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — `addressId` is not a 24-character hex string. UNKNOWN_FIELD — the body carried a field this endpoint does not accept, such as a price, a total, `governorate`, `couponCode` or `userId`.

403.description: FORBIDDEN — checkout belongs to CUSTOMER accounts.

404.description: ADDRESS_NOT_FOUND — `addressId` is not one of your saved addresses. The same answer for an address belonging to another customer and one that does not exist.

post.description:
Creates one order from the signed-in customer cart, atomically: stock is decremented, the
inventory ledger is written, the order is stored and the cart is emptied — **all in a
single MongoDB transaction**. Any failure rolls back every part of it, so there is no state
in which stock moved but no order exists, or the cart emptied but placement failed.

### The client is authoritative for nothing that costs money

The body carries the **id of one of your saved addresses** and an optional note. That is
all. There is no `items`, no `price`, no `total`, no `currency`, no `status`, no `userId`
and no `shippingAddress` field, and sending one returns `400 UNKNOWN_FIELD`. The item list
comes from the server cart, prices from the catalogue, shipping from the server rate
policy, identity from the token, and the status from the server.

### The delivery address

Send `addressId` from `GET /users/me/addresses`. It is resolved **inside the placement
transaction**, through a query that names your account as well as the address, so an
address belonging to somebody else is never selected — it returns `404 ADDRESS_NOT_FOUND`,
the same answer an id that exists nowhere gets.

The address is then **copied onto the order**. Editing or deleting the saved address
afterwards does not change this order by one character, and the order stays fully
renderable even after the address is gone.

### Idempotency — read this before implementing retries

`Idempotency-Key` is **mandatory**; without it the request is rejected `400`. A timeout does
not tell you whether the server committed, so retry with the SAME key and one of two things
happens, both correct:

- the original attempt had committed — you receive **200** with that exact order;
- it had not — the retry places the order and you receive **201**.

**The response body is identical in both cases**, so treat any 2xx as success and parse one
model. Two concurrent requests with one key produce **one** order; the loser receives the
winner result. A key is bound to the account that first used it and to the request body it
was first used with — replaying it with a different address returns `409`, and a key
belonging to another account is refused without revealing anything about it.

Keys are remembered for 24 hours. Beyond that a replay still cannot create a second order:
`orders.idempotencyKey` is unique permanently.

### Failures worth handling explicitly

- `422 CART_EMPTY` — nothing to order.
- `409 OUT_OF_STOCK` — someone bought it first. `details` names the SKU and what is left.
  Nothing was reserved and nothing was charged; refresh the quote.
- `409 PRODUCT_UNAVAILABLE` — a line was delisted or removed.
- `409 CONCURRENT_MODIFICATION` — retrying with the same key is safe.

`pricing.shippingFee` is computed by the server from the chosen address and the order
value. It is `0` under the current configuration, which is the honest number rather than a
promotional one — the per-governorate rate table is unresolved business input. Payment is
Cash on Delivery: nothing is charged now, and `payment.status` stays `PENDING` until the
courier collects.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: A UUID identifying THIS checkout attempt. **Required.** Generate one when the customer opens the confirmation screen, and send the SAME value on every retry of that attempt — after a timeout, a dropped connection or a double tap. Generate a NEW one only for a genuinely new order.

200.description: IDEMPOTENT REPLAY — this key had already created an order, which is returned unchanged. Identical body to the 201.

201.description: The order was created by THIS request.

400.description: MISSING_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY — the header was absent. VALIDATION_ERROR — the key is not a UUID, or `addressId` is not a 24-character hex string. UNKNOWN_FIELD — the body carried a price, total, item list, status, userId, or an inline `shippingAddress` object.

403.description: FORBIDDEN — orders are placed by CUSTOMER accounts. ACCOUNT_DISABLED.

404.description: ADDRESS_NOT_FOUND — `addressId` is not one of your saved addresses. Deliberately the same answer for an address that belongs to another customer and one that does not exist.

409.description: OUT_OF_STOCK — insufficient stock; `details` names the SKU and the available quantity. PRODUCT_UNAVAILABLE — a line is delisted or deleted. IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED — this key was already used for a different request, or by another account. CONCURRENT_MODIFICATION — a transient race; retry with the same key.

422.description: CART_EMPTY — there is nothing in the cart to order.

get.description:
The signed-in customer’s own order history, **newest first**, paginated. Never anybody
else’s: the account is taken from the token and is part of the database query, so there
is no parameter that could widen it.

### Ordering and pagination

Sorted by `placedAt` descending, with the order id as a tie-breaker. That second key
matters: two orders placed in the same millisecond would otherwise have no defined
relative order, and a row could appear on two pages or on none. The ordering here is
stable across requests, so paging through it is safe.

Standard offset pagination: `?page=1&limit=24` (`limit` 1–100). `meta.total` is the TRUE
match count across all pages — use `meta.hasNext` to decide whether to load more.

### Filtering

`?status=` is repeatable and matches ANY of the given values, so one request backs an
"active orders" tab: `?status=PLACED&status=CONFIRMED&status=SHIPPED`. Omit it for every
status. An unrecognised value is a `400`, never a silently empty page.

### What a row contains

A deliberately compact card: id, order number, status, payment, the full money breakdown,
item counts, a thumbnail and the date. Line items, the delivery address and the customer
block are on the detail endpoint — call `GET /orders/{id}` for those.

Every value comes from the order’s own immutable snapshot. Nothing here is read from the
catalogue, so a product that was renamed, repriced or deleted after the order cannot
change this list.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based page number.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Items per page, 1–100.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: Filter by lifecycle status. Repeatable — `?status=PLACED&status=CONFIRMED` matches EITHER, so one request can back an "active orders" tab. Omit it for every status. An unrecognised value is a `400`, not a silent empty page.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — a bad `page`, `limit` or `status` value. UNKNOWN_FIELD — an undocumented query parameter, including any attempt to send `userId`.

403.description: FORBIDDEN — order history belongs to CUSTOMER accounts.

get.description:
The complete customer-facing detail for ONE of the signed-in customer’s orders: line
items, the money breakdown, payment, and the delivery address the goods were sent to.

The response is the **same `OrderDto`** that `POST /orders` returns, so the order-success
screen and the order-detail screen generate and share a single Dart model.

### 404 covers two cases on purpose

An order that does not exist and an order belonging to another customer return exactly the
same response. There is no way to tell them apart, which is the point — a `403` would
confirm that an id is real and turn this endpoint into an oracle for other people’s orders.

### Everything is a snapshot

The line items are what was actually sold: the name, SKU, slug, image and unit price AS OF
the moment the order was placed. They are stored on the order and no product is read to
serve this request. **Never re-fetch a product to render an order** — a catalogue price is
not what the customer agreed to pay, and a deleted product must not break their receipt.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The order id, as returned by `POST /orders` or `GET /orders`.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — `id` is not a 24-character hex id.

404.description: ORDER_NOT_FOUND — no such order, OR it belongs to another customer. Deliberately the same answer for both.

post.description:
Cancels an order the signed-in customer placed, and **returns its stock to the catalogue**
— the status change, the history entry, the stock restoration and the inventory ledger
entries all commit in a **single MongoDB transaction**, or none of them do.

### Only before dispatch

Cancellation is possible while the order is `PLACED` or `CONFIRMED`. Once it is `SHIPPED`
the goods are with the courier and the answer is `409 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE`; the correct
path from there is a failed delivery or a return, both driven by the shop. Show the cancel
button only for those two statuses, and treat the 409 as the authority rather than trusting
a status the client may have been holding for a while.

### Sending it twice is safe

The second request returns `409 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE` with `details` naming the current
status — **not** a second cancellation. Stock is restored exactly once no matter how many
times the request arrives, or how many arrive simultaneously. There is no
`Idempotency-Key` here and none is needed: unlike placement, a repeat cannot create a
second anything.

### Response

The canonical `OrderDto` — the same model `POST /orders` and `GET /orders/{id}` return —
with `status: "CANCELLED"` and the `cancellation` block populated. Re-render from it
directly rather than re-fetching.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The order id, as returned by `POST /orders` or `GET /orders`.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — `id` is not a 24-character hex id, or `reason` is missing, too short or too long. UNKNOWN_FIELD — the body carried a field other than `reason`, including any attempt to send a `status`.

403.description: FORBIDDEN — cancellation is a CUSTOMER action. ACCOUNT_DISABLED.

404.description: ORDER_NOT_FOUND — no such order, OR it belongs to another customer. Deliberately the same answer for both.

409.description: ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE — the order has already been dispatched, delivered, returned, or was already cancelled. `details` names the current status. Do NOT retry — this never succeeds. CONCURRENT_MODIFICATION — the order changed status during this request; re-read it and decide again.

get.description:
Every order in the system, **newest first**, paginated — the screen an operator works
from. Same page shape, same pagination contract and same card model as the customer’s own
history, so there is one order-summary type rather than two that drift.

Filter by lifecycle status to get a work list: `?status=PLACED` is the confirmation queue,
`?status=CONFIRMED` is ready-to-ship, `?status=DELIVERY_FAILED` is the exception queue.
`?status=` is repeatable and matches ANY of the given values.

Search with `?q=`. It matches the order number and the customer SNAPSHOT recorded on
the order — name, email and phone — so an order is still findable by the name on its
delivery note after that customer has changed their name. The term is ESCAPED before
it reaches the database: regular-expression syntax in it matches itself.

Narrow by date with `?placedFrom=` and `?placedTo=`. A date with no time as `placedTo`
means the END of that day in UTC, so `?placedTo=2026-09-03` includes the third.

Ordering is `?sort=`: `newest` (the default), `oldest`, `total_high`, `total_low`.
Every option is served by an index and every one breaks ties on the order id, so
paging is stable and a row cannot appear on two pages or on none.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based page number.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Items per page, 1–100.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: Filter by lifecycle status. Repeatable — `?status=PLACED&status=CONFIRMED` matches EITHER, so one request can back an "active orders" tab. Omit it for every status. An unrecognised value is a `400`, not a silent empty page.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Free text, matched against the order number and the customer SNAPSHOT on the order — name, email and phone. The order number and email match from the start; the name matches anywhere; the phone matches on digits alone, so `010-1234` and `0101234` are the same search. The term is escaped before it reaches the database, so regular expression syntax in it is matched literally. Whitespace-only is not a filter.

parameters.name: placedFrom
parameters.description: Only orders placed at or after this instant. Accepts a date (`2026-09-01`) or a full ISO 8601 timestamp. Interpreted in UTC.

parameters.name: placedTo
parameters.description: Only orders placed at or before this instant. A DATE with no time means the END of that day in UTC, so `2026-09-03` includes everything placed on the third.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Ordering. Every option is served by an index and every one breaks ties on the order id, so paging through the queue cannot skip or repeat a row.

400.description: VALIDATION_ERROR — a bad `page`, `limit` or `status` value. UNKNOWN_FIELD — an undocumented query parameter.

403.description: FORBIDDEN — lifecycle operations require an ADMIN or SUPER_ADMIN account.

get.description:
One row of numbers for the queue tiles, in a single request.

It replaces asking for seven pages of one order each and reading `meta.total` off every
response. That cost seven index scans to draw one row — but the real defect was that the
seven numbers were taken at seven different instants, so an order confirmed midway
through could be counted twice or not at all, and the tiles would not add up to the
total beside them. This is one aggregation at one instant, so they always do.

Every lifecycle status is present, including the ones nothing is in: a status with no
orders has a count of `0` rather than being omitted. A console cannot otherwise tell
"no cancelled orders" from "the count could not be read", and on a fulfilment screen
those are very different sentences.

info.title: Nest Electronics API
info.description:
REST API for the Nest Electronics storefront, admin and mobile clients.

### Conventions

- **Base path** `/api/v1`. Within `v1` the contract is additive-only: new optional
  fields and new endpoints may appear, but nothing is removed, renamed or retyped.
- **Envelope** — success is `{ "data": … }`, plus `"meta"` on collections and
  `"facets"` on product search. Every error is `{ "error": { code, message, … } }`,
  so a client branches on which key is present.
- **`error.code` is a stable enum — switch on it.** `error.message` is human-facing
  and may change between releases; never parse it.
- **Money** is always `{ amount, currency, formatted }` where `amount` is an integer
  in minor units (piastres). `formatted` is for display only. Clients never do money
  arithmetic — every total comes from the server.
- **`POST /orders` requires an `Idempotency-Key` header** and is safe to retry with
  the same key: `201` when the retry created the order, `200` when an earlier attempt
  already had. The body is identical, so treat any 2xx as success.
- **IDs** are 24-character MongoDB ObjectId hex strings, opaque to clients.
- **Dates** are ISO 8601 UTC with `Z`.
- **Nulls** — optional fields are `null`, never omitted, so Dart models stay stable.
- **Enums** are `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` strings.
- **Localised text** is resolved server-side from `Accept-Language` (`en` or `ar`,
  defaulting to `en`). Clients receive plain strings, never `{ en, ar }`.
- **`X-Request-Id`** is echoed on every response and appears in `error.requestId`.
  Quote it in a bug report and the server-side cause can be found directly.
- **Unknown query parameters are rejected with `400 UNKNOWN_FIELD`.** This is a
  security control, so send only documented parameters.


### Authentication

- Endpoints marked with a padlock require `Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>`.
- Obtain the pair from `POST /auth/login`; the access token lives 15 minutes.
- On `401 TOKEN_EXPIRED`, call `POST /auth/refresh` ONCE with the refresh token,
  store the new pair, and retry the original request. A second 401 means sign out.
- `401 REFRESH_TOKEN_REUSED` is terminal — the rotation chain has been revoked as a
  suspected theft. Clear stored tokens and send the user to sign in.
- The whole catalogue is public and needs no token.

It is `0` under the CURRENT configuration — the per-governorate rate table is unresolved business input (OPEN-001), so the server charges nothing rather than inventing a fee. Read this INSTEAD of comparing the amount to zero. `true` means the fee is what the customer owes — including when it is `0` because a free-shipping threshold was met, which must be shown as free delivery. `false` means no rate has been supplied yet (OPEN-001); the accompanying `0` is a placeholder and should be shown as "delivery not yet calculated", never as free. It is `false` under the current configuration and becomes `true` when real per-governorate rates land, WITHOUT the meaning of any other field changing. This field exists precisely so that a client written today keeps telling the truth then: a client that branches on `shippingFee.amount === 0` will misreport every free order.
